96 
Plus: AI hiring is missing women | Tuesday, August 18, 2026
   
 
 View in browser 
   
 
   
 Axios Markets By
Emily Peck and Matt Phillips
 · 
Aug 18, 2026
 
 
 🌮 Let a thousand Tuesday tacos bloom. Tantalizing hints about roaring revenue growth at AI lab Anthropic couldn't keep stocks in the green yesterday. 

 📉 S&P 500 futures are negative premarket, with worries about rising bond yields and the still-closed Strait of Hormuz dominating. 

 🌎 Some analysts point to uncertainty stemming from new leadership at the Federal Reserve for the rise in yields. But it's also a global phenomenon tied to rising oil prices, geopolitical uncertainty and surging demand for capital from both companies and governments.

 Today, Emily is piloting this dirigible solo, bringing us reports on both prices for printed circuit boards — the rigid, resin-based rectangles that computer chips are soldered onto — as well as an update on how AI-related hiring breaks down along gender lines. 

 Forward! In 1,166 words, a 4.5-minute read. 


 
   
   
 
1 big thing: Price pain point 
 
 By Emily Peck 
   
 
 Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics via FRED ; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios The price of one of the most seemingly boring products in the world, bare printed circuit boards, is skyrocketing to levels never seen before.

 Why it matters: AI-driven demand for chips and the war with Iran are two big factors behind the surge . 

 And if you want to understand what's happening with inflation now and what could happen soon, bare printed circuit boards are key. Zoom in: These circuit boards are the "foundational infrastructure of modern electronics," as the director of the printed circuit board lobby group put it last year.

 They're in everything from smartphones and cars to medical and military equipment and dishwashers. In non-industry parlance, these are the green rectangular thingies that they put the silicon chips on. Where it stands: You already know that prices for computer chips are up a lot because data centers, and AI labs need tons of the highest-level memory chips to run their tech. 

 And that demand is driving up prices not only for chips — chipflation! — but also for the boards that they get placed upon, as well. Printed circuit boards became a big flashpoint for supply chain concerns coming out of the pandemic — 90% of them are made in Asia. Lawmakers from both parties have even repeatedly introduced a bill to re-shore production, most recently in May . By the numbers: The producer price index for the boards rose 45% in July from the same time last year. 

 These are the prices domestic producers of circuit boards charge. The U.S. produces only about 4% of the world's supply. But the number is still illustrative of the pricing squeeze being felt globally. The intrigue: The proposed legislation wouldn't be of much help now because the war has pushed up prices for board inputs , or what's used to make them, primarily resin and copper. 

 A major manufacturer of resin in Saudi Arabia was knocked offline in April after an Iranian attack, and it's unclear if it is operational yet . This one plant makes 70% of the world's high-purity polyphenylene ether resin, per CNBC . Prices for electronics are already moving higher — see the chart below — but experts warn we've only begun to feel these shocks. The price gains have helped drive up the shares of the biggest memory chipmakers by triple-digit percentages. Flashback: The situation is similar to what we were seeing when pandemic-driven issues were raising costs for manufacturers and other businesses in 2020, but inflation only started hitting in 2021.

 "It takes at least six months, if not a year, for these price increases fairly far upstream in the supply chain to start to make their way to end users," says Jason Miller, a professor of supply-chain management at Michigan State University's business school. A lot of suppliers have already locked in pricing through contracts. "This is why 2022 was a bloodbath from a pricing standpoint," Miller says. "Because you had all these price increases in 2021. A lot of them didn't really start getting passed on till '22, and then you had the commodity shock in '22, and a lot of that wasn't really felt until '23, even."

 Yes, but: A major difference this time is the labor market. A few years ago, a hiring boom was driving up wages. Labor costs were a big factor in sustaining inflation.

 These days, the labor market is languishing — and that might keep a lid on price increases. Friction point: What's truly mind-blowing is that up until this year, the price of chips and computer stuff has nearly always been a deflationary input. 

 "We've never seen increases like this," Miller says. 
 
 
   
   
 
Bonus chart: Flash surging
 
   
 
 Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics ; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios You're already seeing chipflation feed into the CPI.

 The price of computer software and accessories rose 21.2% in July from the previous year, the largest increase on record, according to the data released last week. 

 Besides software, the category includes memory flash drives — which have seen their prices double over the past year. Reality check: Overall, however, inflation looked pretty benign. As Matt wrote earlier this summer , "few Americans are going to cite the cost of flash drives for breaking their budget."

2. Women are missing out on the AI jobs boom
 
 By Emily Peck 
   
 
 Data: LinkedIn; Table: Danielle Alberti/Axios Women made up just over a quarter of new hires in the U.S. for AI roles last year — compared with half of new hires in non-AI occupations, per new LinkedIn data out this morning.

 Why it matters: These jobs are some of the fastest-growing and highest-paying in the country right now — at a time when the overall labor market is pretty sluggish — and the report shows women are getting left behind.

 By the numbers: Men landed 74%, and women 26%, of the new hires for AI roles in 2025.

 The highest-paying roles typically have higher percentages of men. To get hiring information, the platform looked at user, or member, profiles. For data on compensation it analyzed job listings. Zoom in: An increasingly popular job is called "member of technical staff," a technical role common in AI labs that often sits at the intersection of advanced research and full-stack engineering.

 82% of new hires to these roles went to men in 2025. And this year, the median listed pay is $223,000. The data annotator job, meanwhile, with a median pay of $51,000, is roughly split evenly between men and women. Between the lines: The data confirms what our eyes have been telling us all along. Most of the public faces of the AI buildout have been men. 

 Yes, but: The AI sector might make up a huge and growing part of the economy, but the jobs themselves are just a small sliver of the labor market.

 The bottom line: Women have long been underrepresented in the tech industry, particularly in leadership and technical roles. The AI boom is widening the divide.

 "Women may be included in the AI economy, but not in the roles most likely to drive long-term economic mobility, leadership, and decision-making power," Sarah Steinberg, head of global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn, said in an email to Axios.
